Are there any real studies on shaming?

I'm not sure how a study like that could be done, methodologically speaking.

I would like to see a compiled list of first hand accounts in which an incident of shaming caused someone to take an honest look at themselves and make the changes that bettered their life. I've seen several, but it would be a cool resource if it was compiled together at one site.

It would probably involve participants being given unhealthy food, and exposing them to shaming, and then seeing if there's any correlation with the amount (if any) of junk food they eat as compared to the control.

Pretty much all of it is done through questionnaires of self-reporting, which is why often times studies will say "perceived [shaming]" or "negative perceived X" or the like, as they cannot claim participants were actually stigmatized in reality, and they cannot claim cause/effect and because these studies can only evaluate correlation. Considering how frequent people lie about their diets, even in a private setting with their doctors, I'm also skeptic of the results of these studies. If you want to look into it more, better search engine terminology would probably be phrases like "weight stigma"

It would be interesting to see what the results are of studies that target former fat people who actually lost weight and kept it off long term, to see what factors motivated them to make a lifestyle eating change.

Edit: Oh yeah, a lot of the studies looking into the relationship of "weight stigma" and things like depression/weight gain/weight loss/etc rarely ever touch on the factor of addiction, or food addiction, which IMO could have just as huge an influence on weight loss goal outcomes, more so than "perceived negative" attitudes/judgment by others.

Yeah, and most of these "studies" just focus on the fact that the person FEELS like they have been discriminated against because of their weight and that those people gain weight, this does not take in consideration that this person might have a distorted perception of reality and/or attribute everything negative to discrimination due to their weight, self-victimization plays a big role in this

Probably.

I've been involved in a lot of studies that study reactions to various stimuli (ex. sexual competitors) in relation to consumer behavior, impulse control, how it all correlates to ovulation cycle, employee reaction to different types of motivation, etc.

The biggest problem with academic works, as opposed to applied research, is that you can pretty much publish anything you want with any conclusion you want no matter how shoddy the study is designed and stats tweaked. Nobody really notices, so it has attracted a lot of activists and/or people lying about their research simply to justify the continued funding of their research.

Sifting through everything to find what is legit is a nightmare.

Edit: The research on how people react to the notion of moderation is very interesting as well, but it's not the same across the board as it is relative to individual's recent behavior.
